name: Alagoas
summary_text: Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. Alagoas stands under that national framework: state law does not displace the constitutional and federal provisions described below.  After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.  Killing risk is measurable and Alagoas is recorded in the national tally. ANTRA's 9th annual dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counted 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of roughly 34% year-on-year, leaving the country first in world rankings; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence, and Alagoas accounted for 2 of those 80 killings. The preceding dossier, reported by CNN Brasil on 27 January 2025, counted 122 people killed in 2024, 16% below 2023, with Alagoas accounting for 6 of them.  Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.

name: Amapa
summary_text: Amapá stands under Brazil's national framework, and no state-level deviation affecting a visitor is documented in the sources. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted 14-1, and joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015. Legal gender change has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018, and gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, docketed as ADO 26 and MI 4733, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. That ruling is the operative basis on which homophobia and transphobia are treated as criminal conduct, and an expat legal guide confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry.  Documents remain binary. There is no third-gender option in national identity documents, although civil-registry entries recording 'non-binary/unspecified' have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of registry entries to a neutral gender and stands as precedent for further cases.  The protective text does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview records that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, and that these advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Enforcement of the anti-discrimination provisions is uneven in practice, and smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights, a factor that bears on a visitor moving through Amapá's less urbanised territory.
